questions.question: A team agrees a feature is worth building and adds it to the quarter's plan. Nothing else on the plan changes. What has actually happened?
options: A commitment, because leadership approved it in a decision forum
A preference, because no capacity was withdrawn from anything else
A commitment, because the plan is the team's binding record
A prioritization, because the item now sits above other items
questions.explanation: Capacity is finite, so a real commitment always removes something. If nothing was removed, the team agreed the idea was good. Option A is the tempting one: approval feels like the moment of commitment, and it is the moment most teams point to. But approval without displacement leaves four workstreams each running at a fraction, which is what the plan will show in three months.

questions.question: A PM is confident a feature will work for the target population, but engineering has never touched the subsystem it depends on and cannot say what is in there. What does this state require?
options: Commit with a wide date range so the uncertainty is disclosed
Commit, since value conviction is what determines whether work is worth doing
Do not commit yet; spend a bounded slice retiring the effort unknown first
Reduce scope until engineering is willing to give a firm estimate
questions.explanation: Strong value conviction with weak effort conviction is the second row of the table, and the correct move is to buy effort knowledge before committing. Option A is the answer a careful PM gives after learning the vocabulary: it discloses the uncertainty honestly but still hands the organization a date that other people plan against. Option D is worse, because a firm estimate extracted under pressure is not effort conviction.

questions.question: Noted's core dependency loses support in ten weeks. A PM writes a commitment brief for the migration that opens with the user value the migration will deliver. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing; every commitment should be justified by user value
The user value should be quantified rather than described
Migration work should be committed by engineering, not by product
Forced work has no value bet to argue about, so the invented story then competes for attention as if it were evidence
questions.explanation: This is the boundary of the model. The honest frame for forced work is consequence exposure over time, not user outcome. Option A is tempting because 'always tie work to user value' is a rule most PMs are taught, and it is usually right. Here it manufactures a story that will be cited later as though someone had evidence for it.

questions.question: Three enterprise customers request a feature. Their combined contracts are about 20% of revenue. All three requests came through the same account manager in one month. Which conclusion does this evidence support?
options: That the problem is widespread among enterprise team leads
That the requested solution is the right one for the underlying problem
That three named accounts asked, through one channel, and that a revenue relationship is exposed
That the feature should be committed, because revenue concentration outweighs sample concerns
questions.explanation: The requests establish that three accounts asked and that a commercial relationship carries risk. They do not establish prevalence, mechanism, or solution fit, because one channel is not an independent sample. Option D is the answer a commercially minded PM gives: it is not absurd, and account risk is a real input to a commitment. But it moves account risk into the value column, where it will later be quoted as evidence about the problem.

questions.question: A commitment brief names the displaced work as "other roadmap items, which we will fit in around this." What is the specific defect?
options: The displacement is unnamed, so no one has been told their work stopped and the capacity edge has not been found
The brief should list every roadmap item, not a summary
The brief needs an estimate for the displaced items before it can be approved
Fitting work in around a commitment is acceptable if the team has slack
questions.explanation: Displacement is the test that separates a commitment from an intention. 'Fit in around it' means the capacity edge was never located, so it will be found later, at a worse moment, by whoever was quietly depending on the displaced work. Option D is the tempting one because slack does sometimes exist; but a team that believes it has slack has not measured the edge either, and the belief is what fails.
